soil-agri-022.title: Nitrate leaching: fertilizer that slips past the roots
soil-agri-022.text: Human activity now adds 50% more nitrogen to the land than natural sources do, and leached fertilizers and manures make up 75% of that human share. Nitrate leaching is the loss of nitrate from soil as drainage water carries the excess ions down to groundwater, streams and the sea. Soils do not hold them. Farmers place nitrate and ammonium fertilizers in the root zone because plants absorb them easily, but whatever nitrate the crop leaves behind is free to move. How much leaches depends on three things: the soil's type and structure, how much water the crop uses, and how much nitrate is already present. Sandy soils hold little water, so it drains through quickly, while clays hold much. The stakes reach the kitchen tap. Nitrate in drinking water is linked to methemoglobinemia, or blue baby syndrome, so regulators cap it at 45 to 50 mg per litre. One defence is a {{ref:soil-agri-068}}, sown to take up the nitrogen left over from fertilizing the previous crop before it can leach.

soil-agri-034.title: Soil solarization: cooking pests under plastic
soil-agri-034.text: In one study, eight days under plastic killed every Verticillium dahliae fungus 25 cm down. Soil solarization is a non-chemical pest control method that traps the sun's heat in soil until many soil-borne plant pathogens are killed or badly weakened. Moist soil is covered with a tarp, usually clear polyethylene. It must reach 35–60 °C, which kills pathogens in the top 30 cm, and temperatures fall with depth. Fungi, bacteria, nematodes, insect and mite pests, and weeds all suffer. It does not sterilize. It kills up to 90% of pathogens, while heat-tolerant beneficial microbes such as Bacillus survive and recolonize, leaving the soil more resistant to disease. Ordinary plastic covers protect crops in the coldest months; solarization covers soil in the hottest. Katan first described it in detail in 1976, and within thirty years it was applied in more than 60 countries. Concerns include the fate of the plastic, the weaker weed control of biodegradable covers, and reduced microbial richness.

soil-agri-015.title: Drip irrigation: water delivered drop by drop
soil-agri-015.text: Buried clay pots for watering were described in China in the first century BCE, but the modern drip system was invented in Israel. Drip irrigation is micro-irrigation that lets water drip slowly to plant roots, from above or below the surface, placing it in the root zone to minimize evaporation. Properly managed, it can be the most water-efficient method, with field water efficiency typically 80 to 90%. Liquid fertilizer is often mixed into the water, a practice called fertigation, with reported fertilizer savings of up to 95%. Localized watering cuts fertilizer loss by leaching, keeps the root zone at field capacity, and keeps foliage dry against disease. Precision has a catch. So little water leaches that salts build up at the edge of the wetted zone, and regular slight over-watering flushes them below the roots. In 2023, 3% of the world's farmers used drip.

soil-agri-054.title: Integrated pest management: control, not eradication
soil-agri-054.text: Integrated pest management aims to keep pests in check, not to wipe them out. It combines non-chemical and chemical methods to hold pests at tolerable, economic levels while relying less on chemicals. The FAO describes it as integrating biological, chemical, physical and cultural strategies to grow healthy crops while minimizing pesticide use and its risks. Prevention comes first, through resistant varieties, crop rotation and intercropping. Pesticides are used only when needed, often timed to a stage of the pest's life cycle, which also helps protect water quality.

soil-agri-058.title: Crop yield: the harvest per hectare
soil-agri-058.text: A medieval cereal field in the UK gave about 500 kg/ha. The Industrial Revolution raised that to 2000 kg/ha, and the {{ref:soil-agri-138}} to 8000 kg/ha. Crop yield is the amount of a crop, or of a product such as milk or wool, produced per unit area of land. It is usually measured in kilograms per hectare or bushels per acre. Fertilizer, better tools and farming methods, and improved crop varieties drove the rise. Degraded land drags the other way. In 2025 about 1.7 billion people lived in areas with sizeable yield losses from degradation, and in rich countries intensive inputs sustain yields but mask the damage.

soil-agri-010.title: Precision agriculture: farming field by square metre
soil-agri-010.text: In 1985, researchers at the University of Minnesota varied the lime they spread across fields instead of applying one rate. Precision agriculture is a farm management strategy built on data about time, place and individual plants or animals. It fits decisions to variation across fields, for better efficiency, yield and sustainability. The concept emerged in the United States in the early 1980s, and grid sampling at one sample per hectare appeared then too. GPS lets farmers map how yield, topography, organic matter, moisture, nitrogen, pH, electrical conductivity and other soil variables change across a field. A first wave of tools brought satellite and aerial imagery, weather prediction and variable rate fertilizer; a second added precise planting, topographic mapping and soil data. The payoff is the right input in the right place at the right time. That can cut nutrient use while raising yields, which limits nitrogen leaching and protects soils and groundwater. Following GPS guidance lines also reduces soil compaction.

soil-agri-138.title: The Green Revolution and its bill for the soil
soil-agri-138.text: Norman Borlaug, called the father of the Green Revolution, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. The Green Revolution was a period in which technology transfer initiatives produced a large increase in crop yields. It combined high-yielding cereal varieties, expanded irrigation, modern management, hybrid seeds, synthetic fertilizers and pesticides. The new varieties take up more nitrogen and carry semi-dwarfing genes against lodging, the falling over of tall stems. They outperform traditional varieties only with enough irrigation, pesticides and fertilizer. Cereal production in developing nations more than doubled from 1961 to 1985, and a 2021 estimate credits a 44% rise in yields between 1965 and 2010. Wheat bred to tolerate acid, aluminium-rich soils opened the Cerrado savanna to farming. The soil paid. Over-farming caused contamination, erosion and degradation, and nutrient depletion pushed farmers to clear forest. Nitrogen applied beyond crop needs, such as broadcast urea, emits nitrous oxide and pollutes water.

soil-agri-005.title: The rotation effect: why rotated crops yield more
soil-agri-005.text: Crops grown in rotation gain a yield benefit that agronomists simply call the rotation effect. It comes broadly from relieving the drawbacks of monocropping. Better nutrition, less pest, pathogen and weed stress, and better soil structure have been linked to it in some cases. More organic matter improves water infiltration and retention, raising drought tolerance and reducing erosion. Less intensive working of the soil lets microbes thrive, and soil with low microbial activity supplies far fewer nutrients from the same biomass. Over time, rotated crops can meet production goals with fewer purchased inputs.

soil-agri-041.title: Reclaiming sea and swamp for farmland
soil-agri-041.text: Before industrialisation, farming was the main reason people reclaimed land. Agricultural land reclamation turns sea or wetland into farmland. In South China, farmers walled off shore areas near river mouths to make fish ponds, or paddy fields of more salt-tolerant rice. Draining swampy or seasonally flooded wetlands makes productive farmland and also controls mosquitoes. Salt marshes, once dismissed as coastal wastelands, were widely lost to reclamation for agriculture, urban development and salt production.

soil-agri-023.title: Phosphorus leaching: when sorption sites fill up
soil-agri-023.text: Phosphorus leaching is the loss of phosphorus from fields by downward movement through soil. It is an important pathway on flat, sandy land or on soils prone to preferential flow. Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus clings to soil particles, especially iron and aluminium oxides and hydroxides such as gibbsite and ferrihydrite. Soils given more than crops need, often for decades, have these sorption sites filled by 'legacy phosphorus', so new additions leach. Long waterlogging can also release phosphorus by dissolving ferric iron minerals, a concern when restoring drained wetlands. Phosphorus drives {{ref:soil-env-020}} in surface waters, so its loss threatens water quality.

soil-agri-139.title: Coir: the coconut husk that stands in for peat
soil-agri-139.text: One kilogram of dry coco peat swells to 15 litres of moist growing medium. Coir is coconut husk fibre, and its processed form, coco peat, goes into potting mixes as a substitute for peat. Concern over the sustainability of extracting peat has increased its use. It holds water like a sponge and has a pH of 5.5 to 6.5. It is low in nutrients, though, and incompletely decomposed coco peat ties up nitrogen as it breaks down. It is also high in sodium and potassium, so it is buffered with a calcium solution; its potassium can otherwise cause magnesium and calcium deficiencies.

soil-agri-055.title: Land restoration: returning land to an earlier state
soil-agri-055.text: Not every land project aims to make new farmland. Land restoration returns land to a different or earlier state for an intended purpose, which may include renaturalisation or rewilding. It counters human-caused damage such as pollution, deforestation and salination. That sets it apart from land reclamation, which alters or destroys ecosystems for cultivation or construction. Each project chooses a reference ecosystem to judge success and adjusts as the ecosystem responds. Against {{ref:soil-env-072}}, soil is first fixed with grasses and planted rows of trees and shrubs to stop dunes moving, then enriched with nitrogen-fixing plants and rotated crops.

soil-agri-048.title: Herbicide persistence: how long a weed killer lasts
soil-agri-048.text: Some herbicides can leave the ground almost permanently barren. Herbicide persistence is how long a herbicide stays active in soil. Residual activity is low if rain or soil reactions neutralize it within weeks or months, and high if it stays potent for the long term. Each compound's chemistry decides. Atrazine belongs to the triazine family, the herbicides most feared for groundwater contamination. It breaks down slowly in soils above neutral pH, and soil water can carry it to the water table, a 'carryover' effect. Many modern herbicides are formulated to degrade soon after application.

soil-agri-047.title: Soil-applied herbicides that work below ground
soil-agri-047.text: Some herbicides strike before a weed reaches the surface. Soil-applied herbicides are spread before planting or crop emergence, and the roots or shoots of emerging seedlings take them up. Many are absorbed by shoots still underground. EPTC and trifluralin work this way, whereas glyphosate, 2,4-D and dicamba are sprayed on foliage. Placement matters. The chemical must sit in the right soil layer, worked in mechanically or by rainfall. Left on the surface, it is lost to volatilization and photolysis, breakdown by light. Adsorption to soil colloids or organic matter often reduces the amount weeds can absorb.

soil-agri-032.title: Steaming soil clean of weeds and disease
soil-agri-032.text: Modern soil steaming was developed in Germany in 1888 and first used commercially in the United States in 1893. Soil steam sterilization fully or partly sterilizes soil with steam, in open fields or greenhouses. Steam kills weeds, bacteria, fungi and viruses by heating soil enough to inactivate enzymes and coagulate vital cell proteins. In the field it only partly disinfects, because heat-resistant spore-forming bacteria survive and revitalize the soil. True sterilization needs a laboratory autoclave. Today superheated steam at 180–200 °C is often used. It is now considered the best way to disinfect sick soil, potting soil and compost, and an alternative to bromomethane, which the Montreal Protocol curtailed. Steaming also relieves soil fatigue, the decline in fertility under poor management, and frees nutrients locked in the soil. In integrated steaming, an injected compost-based activator recolonizes the soil with beneficial microbes such as Bacillus subtilis.

soil-agri-030.title: Testing a potting mix with a water extract
soil-agri-030.text: A potting mix is not made of soil, yet it can still take a soil test. The saturated media extract is the main test of a mix's chemistry: it analyses a water extract of the mix. Reference levels are clear. Soluble salts are best at 2.0–3.5 mS/cm, with 0.75–5.0 acceptable; nitrate-N should be 100–200 ppm and phosphorus 6–9 ppm. Missing nutrients come from fertilizer: slow-release synthetics in conventional mixes, or compost in organic ones, at most 1 part compost to 1 part bulking material.

soil-agri-029.title: Specialty potting mixes for picky plants
soil-agri-029.text: A cactus and a carnivorous plant want very different pots. Specialty potting mixes are growing media adapted to the needs of a plant, or of a growth stage, for aeration, drainage, nutrition and pH. Cacti and succulents need sharp drainage from a much larger share of perlite or sand. Carnivorous plants prefer the nutrient-poor, acidic soils of bogs and fens. Small seeds start well in light germination mixes, and larger ones in seed-starting mixes. Cuttings root better in soilless mixes such as perlite, vermiculite, sand and sphagnum moss than in water.

soil-agri-024.title: How much salt a crop can take
soil-agri-024.text: Saline land covers 3,230,000 km2 worldwide. A crop's salt tolerance is the highest salt level it can withstand without losing productivity; beyond that it is harmed. The salt level is usually taken as the soil salinity or the salinity of the irrigation water. Tolerance matters most on irrigated land in arid and semi-arid regions, where salinization concerns hundreds of millions of hectares. Salty sprinkler water burns leaves. On one Australian scale, sensitive crops such as almond, apricot and citrus suffer below 178 mg/L chloride. Tolerant ones such as cotton, sorghum and sunflower only above 710 mg/L. Key studies include USDA Agriculture Handbook No. 60 in 1954, Maas and Hoffman's extensive study over 20 years later, and an FAO worldwide survey in 2002. Most data come from pots, drums or lysimeters under controlled conditions, and field data are rarer. Much research now aims to breed crops with higher salt tolerance for salinity-stricken regions.

soil-agri-038.title: Agrominerals, the rocks that feed plants
soil-agri-038.text: Rock that feeds plants has a nickname: stone bread. Agrominerals are minerals that matter to farming and horticulture because they can supply essential plant nutrients. Natural or processed, they serve as alternative fertilizers or soil amendments, and the term dates from the 19th century. Their use began with small fixes: perlite for aeration, pumice to curb evaporation, and vermiculite and zeolite to store moisture. Potash, a major source of potassium, was one of the original agrominerals. Its finite supply drives prices up, so research now seeks alternatives.

soil-agri-036.title: Agrogeology: geology put to work for farmers
soil-agri-036.text: In 1989, the Tanzania-Canada project helped farmers in southern Tanzania find and test local raw materials for their fields. It was the first agrogeology project with major funding. Agrogeology is the study of agrominerals, their origins and uses; more broadly, it is geology applied to farm soil productivity and health. It combines geology, soil science, agronomy and chemistry, using geological resources to improve the chemical and physical properties of soil. Agrogeologists work to replenish fertility where unsustainable farming has depleted agrominerals. The idea is not new: raw materials have been used as fertilizer since the 1800s. The toolkit is varied. Apatite releases phosphate slowly in acid soils, carbonates lime the soil, malachite cures copper deficiency, scoria serves as a water-saving mulch and zeolite conserves nitrogen.

soil-agri-012.title: Within-field variability: no field is uniform
soil-agri-012.text: No field is the same from one end to the other. Within-field variability is the difference in growing conditions within and between fields, which {{ref:soil-agri-010}} measures and manages. It arises from climate (hail, drought, rain), from soils (texture, depth, nitrogen levels), from cropping practices, and from weeds and disease. Permanent indicators, chiefly soil properties, describe a field's constants. Point indicators track crop status such as disease, water stress or nitrogen stress. Weather stations, sensors measuring soil electrical resistivity, and satellite imagery supply much of this information.
